Outline: 

--- 

Today we are going to consider _alternate_ linear classifiers. Recall that, in 
regression, we defined a method by a combination of loss function (MSE, MAE, 
*etc*) and function class (linear, polynomial, *etc.*). As a result, we would
fit many different linear models to the same data set and they were all 
optimal / correct under some different set of assumptions. 

The same phenomenon will hold here for _linear_ classifiers as well: for each
of the methods discussed in these notes, we will still have a _linear_ decision
boundary, like logistic regression, but they will be defined by different
objective functions. A key difference from the regression context is that we
don't typically truly care about these loss functions; the things we might
care about (minimizing FNR subject to a FPR constraint) don't really play
nicely with optimization. Instead, we use a surrogate loss function and tune
parameters (both the decision threshold and more traditional things like a
$\lambda$ regularization strength parameter) to optimize for the downstream
things we actually care about. 

That is to say, it is perfectly reasonable and indeed quite common to do 
something like this for 'ridge logistic regression'

- Split data into three parts--$\Dcal_1, \Dcal_2, \Dcal_3$--for parameter fitting,
  hyperparemeter selection, and final accuracy estimation respectively. 
- Fit ridge logistic regression at a variety of $\lambda$ values on $\Dcal_1$,
  recording $\hat{\bbeta}_{\lambda}$ for each $\lambda$: 
  
  $$\begin{align*}
  \hat{\bbeta}_{\lambda_1} &= \argmin_{\bbeta} \text{LogisticLoss}(\bbeta; \Dcal_1) + \frac{\lambda_1}{2} \|\bbeta\|_2^2 \\
  \hat{\bbeta}_{\lambda_2} &= \argmin_{\bbeta} \text{LogisticLoss}(\bbeta; \Dcal_1) + \frac{\lambda_K}{2} \|\bbeta\|_2^2\\
  \dots \\
  \hat{\bbeta}_{\lambda_K} &= \argmin_{\bbeta} \text{LogisticLoss}(\bbeta; \Dcal_1) + \frac{\lambda_K}{2} \|\bbeta\|_2^2
  \end{align*}$$
- For each $\hat{\bbeta}_{\lambda_k}$, compute a false positive rate and false
  negative rate on $\Dcal_2$: call these $\text{FPR}_{\lambda_k}, \text{FNR}_{\lambda_k}$
  respectively
- Pick the $\lambda$ that minimizes FNR subject to a FPR constraint: 

  $$\lambda_* = \argmin_{\lambda \in \{\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_K\}} \begin{cases} \text{FNR}_{\lambda_k} & \text{ if } \text{FPR}_{\lambda_k} < \alpha \\ \infty & \text{ otherwise } \end{cases}$$
  
- Estimate final FNR, FPR on $\Dcal_3$

Here we have *tuned* for something that wasn't actually the loss function used
to define our method. This is totally reasonable! While 'direct' optimization
of the thing we care about is nice, when its not possible, strategies like this
are perfectly fine.

(Aside: we always had this option in regression as well: we could have optimized
ridge-OLS to minimize MAE, but just as a practical matter, it's faster, easier, 
and better to just fit LAD directly.)

So with all of this said, what are the different methods we might choose to 
create? 

## Discriminative vs Generative

Historically, linear classifiers have been divided into two broad camps: 

- Generative Classifiers
- Discriminative Classifiers

Here 'discriminative' doesn't refer to bias or prejudice; just the older sense
of 'able to tell things apart'. Both of these will ultimately result in 
linear decision boundaries, but they get there from different starting points. 

Discriminative classifiers are more similar to what we saw in the regression
context: 

- We take $\bX$ as a given, assume that $Y$ depends on it somehow, and directly
  minimize a loss function to 'fit' that relationship. 
  
The only modeling choice here is how we relate $\bX$ and $Y$ or, equivalently,
the loss function we use in our optimization problem. 

As we saw last time, logistic regression is an instance of this type of classifier.
In particular, recall that we built logistic regression out of a tripartite
_generalized_ linear model. 

$$\begin{align*}
\eta &= \bx^{\top}\bbeta \tag{Linear Predictor} \\
\mu  &= \text{logistic adapter}(\eta) \tag{Link/Adapter Term}\\
     &= \frac{e^{\eta}}{1+e^{\eta}} \\
     &= \frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta}} \\
     &= \textsf{SoftMax}(\eta, 0) \\
Y    &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(\mu) \tag{Sampling/Observation Model}
\end{align*}$$

But how can we actually build an optimization problem here? Well, let's
first 'collapse' terms so that we can put this whole model on one line: 

$$Y \sim \text{Bernoulli}\left(\frac{1}{1+e^{-\bx^{\top}\bbeta}}\right)$$

When faced with a statistical model like this, a common strategy is to use
a _maximum likelihood_ estimation procedure. That is, we pick the $\bbeta$
that 'fit our data best' in the sense of giving us the _highest_ probability
of seeing what we saw.[^mle] Note that we can write the general Bernoulli
probability mass function (PMF) as: 

$$Z\sim\text{Bernoulli}(p) \Leftrightarrow \P(Z = z) = p^z(1-p)^{1-z} =\begin{cases} p & z = 1 \\ 1- p & z = 0 \end{cases}$$

With the above, this gives us: 

$$\begin{align*}
\P(Y = y_i | \bX = \bx_i) &= \left(\frac{1}{1+e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}}\right)^{y_i}\left(1 - \frac{1}{1+e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}}\right)^{1-y_i} \\
&= \left(\frac{1}{1+e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}}\right)^{y_i}\left( \frac{e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}}{1+e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}}\right)^{1-y_i} \\
&= \frac{(e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta})^{1-y_i}}{1+e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}} \\
&= \frac{e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta(1-y_i)}}{1+e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}} \\
\end{align*}$$

If we multiply this across $n$ IID observations, we get a joint PMF of 

$$\P(\bbeta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta(1-y_i)}}{1+e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}}$$

so we can fit logistic regression by just solving the following problem: 

$$\hat{\bbeta}_{\text{Logistic}} = \argmax_{\bbeta}\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta(1-y_i)}}{1+e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}}$$

Easy, right? 

No, not really. This is _conceptually_ complete, but practically it's a huge
pain. When we multiply many probabilities together, we get _very_ small
numbers which can make a computer struggle. We like the 'average' look of ERMs, 
not this weird product structure. And we like to think about _minimizing loss_
instead of maximizing probability. 

Thankfully, a little bit of mathematical slight of hand here will help us out:

$$\argmax_{x} f(x) \Leftrightarrow \argmin_{x} -\frac{1}{n}\log f(f)$$

(Convince yourself that this is true!)

Applying this to our problem above, we get: 

$$\begin{align*}
\hat{\bbeta}_{\text{Logistic}} &= \argmax_{\bbeta}\prod_{i=1}^n \frac{e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta(1-y_i)}}{1+e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}} \\
&= \argmax_{\bbeta}\log \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta(1-y_i)}}{1+e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}} \\
&=\argmax_{\bbeta}\sum_{i=1}^n \log\left[ \frac{e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta(1-y_i)}}{1+e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}}\right] \\
&=\argmax_{\bbeta}\sum_{i=1}^n -\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta(1-y_i) - \log\left[ 1+e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}\right] \\
&=\argmin_{\bbeta}\sum_{i=1}^n \bx_i^{\top}\bbeta(1-y_i) + \log\left[ 1+e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}\right] \\
&=\argmin_{\bbeta}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \bx_i^{\top}\bbeta(1-y_i) + \log\left[ 1+e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}\right] \\
&=\argmin_{\bbeta}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n -y_i\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta + \bx_i^{\top}\bbeta + \log\left[ 1+e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}\right] \\
&= \argmin_{\bbeta}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n -y_i\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta + \log[e^{\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}] + \log\left[ 1+e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}\right] \\
&= \argmin_{\bbeta}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n -y_i\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta + \log\left[e^{\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}*(1+e^{-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta})\right] \\
&= \argmin_{\bbeta}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n -y_i\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta + \log\left[e^{\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}+e^{\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}\right] \\
&= \argmin_{\bbeta}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n -y_i\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta + \log\left[1 + e^{\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}\right] \\
&= \argmin_{\bbeta}\E_{\text{Training Data}} \text{Logistic Loss}(\bbeta; y_i, \bx_i) \\
\end{align*}$$

Whew... So we see that logistic regression is (after quite some work!) just 
another ERM with a funny loss. This particular loss is sometimes known as 
*binomial deviance* or *cross entropy loss*, but I just like to call it the 
logistic loss as that makes the original source the most clear. 

This loss function can seem a bit opaque - what is it actually doing? Let's
take it case by case: 

- when $y_i=0$, the first term is zero, so we just want to *minimize* $\log(1 + e^{\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta})$. Note that $\log(1+e^x)\approx x$ for $x$ not too small,
  so this is really just minimizing $\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta$.
  Hence, the optimization problem tries to push $\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta$ smaller
  for observations where $y_i=0$
- when $y_i=1$, the first term is bigger, and *minimizing* $-\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta$
  encourages us to make $\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta$ larger for observations where $y_i=1$

Hence, under all the funny math and weird signs, the directions really do
work out the way we'd expect. 

In some other contexts, if we use $y = \pm 1$ instead of $y \in \{0, 1\}$, the
same math can be shown to work out to 

$$\argmin_{\bbeta}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \log\left[1 + e^{-y_i\bx_i^{\top}\bbeta}\right]$$

which is maybe a bit cleaner, even if it leaves the 'Bernoulli'-structure less
evident.

But this is still a bit opaque: graphing things make it even clearer. Let's
plot $\alpha = \hat{y}y$. So $\alpha \to 1$ when $y = 1$ and our probability
is large ('confident and correct') or $y=-1$ and our probability is small;
in the case where $y=1$ but our 'score' is close to $-1$, we get a
negative number ('confidently wrong'). Graphically this looks something like
this: 

```{r}
#| echo: false
alpha <- seq(-3, 3, length.out=201)
acc     <- function(alpha) ifelse(alpha < 0, 1, 0)
lr_loss <- function(alpha) log(1 + exp(-2*alpha))

plot(alpha, acc(alpha), type="l",
     xlab=expression(alpha==y * hat(y)),
     ylab="Loss", 
     main="Classification Losses", 
     ylim=c(0, 5))
lines(alpha, lr_loss(alpha), col="red4")
legend("topright", 
       col=c("black", "red4"), 
       lwd=2, 
       legend=c("Accuracy", "Logistic Regression"))
```

This is interesting! We see that the loss function we might 'really' care
about (pure accuracy) has the 'flatness' problem we previously saw with 
$\ell_0$ penalties and best subsets; that's why we can't really just say
'maximize accuracy' directly. But the logistic loss is sort of a
nice convex (everywhere upwards facing) approximation. 

Are there others we could use? Clearly yes, we could use a sort of 'one-sided'
absolute value like this: 

```{r}
alpha <- seq(-3, 3, length.out=201)
acc     <- function(alpha) ifelse(alpha < 0, 1, 0)
lr_loss <- function(alpha) log(1 + exp(-2*alpha))
hinge_loss <- function(alpha) pmax(0, 1-alpha)

plot(alpha, acc(alpha), type="l",
     xlab=expression(alpha == y * hat(y)),
     ylab="Loss", 
     main="Classification Losses", 
     ylim=c(0, 5))
lines(alpha, lr_loss(alpha), col="red4")
lines(alpha, hinge_loss(alpha), col="green4")
legend("topright", 
       col=c("black", "red4", "green4"), 
       lwd=2, 
       legend=c("Accuracy", "Logistic Regression", "Hinge Loss"))
```

where here the green line is given by $$(1 - \alpha)_+ = \begin{cases} 1 - \alpha & \text{ when } 1 - \alpha > 0 \\ 0 & \text{ when } 1 - \alpha \leq 0 \end{cases}$$
Here, $(x)_+ = \max\{0, x\}$ is known as the *positive part* operator. 

Where does this *hinge loss* come from?

## Generative Classifiers

Our other big set of classifiers are so called *generative* classifiers. These
start for a model for $\bX$ from $y$ -- the 'reverse' of our usual model -- and
then uses Bayes' Rule to 'invert the reverse' and get a forward model. (You might
remember that Bayes rule was referred to as the *Law of Inverse Probability*
in the early days as it does exactly this.) We actually already saw a toy
generative classifier in our earlier notes, so let's talk about what these 
might look like in a more significant application. 

If we fit a bivariate normal distribution to the body mass and flipper length
of each of our three penguin species, we might get something like this: 

```{r}
#| echo: false
# TODO: Fix this up. AI over complex nonsense follows...
library(tidyverse)
library(mvtnorm)

# 1. Clean data and define grid bounding box
df <- penguins |>
    drop_na(body_mass, flipper_len, species)

grid_x <- seq(min(df$body_mass) - 200, max(df$body_mass) + 200, length.out = 150)
grid_y <- seq(min(df$flipper_len) - 5, max(df$flipper_len) + 5, length.out = 150)
eval_grid <- expand_grid(body_mass = grid_x, flipper_len = grid_y)

# 2. Fit 2D normal parameters (MLE) per species and evaluate density on the grid
density_df <- df |>
    nest(.by = species) |>
    mutate(
        mu = map(data, \(d) colMeans(d[, c("body_mass", "flipper_len")])),
        sigma = map(data, \(d) cov(d[, c("body_mass", "flipper_len")])),
        grid = map2(mu, sigma, \(m, s) {
            eval_grid |>
                mutate(density = dmvnorm(eval_grid, mean = m, sigma = s))
        })
    ) |>
    select(species, grid) |>
    unnest(grid)

# 3. Plot contours with observations
ggplot() +
    geom_point(
        data = df,
        aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len, color = species),
        alpha = 0.45,
        size = 1.5
    ) +
    geom_contour(
        data = density_df,
        aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len, z = density, color = species),
        bins = 7,
        linewidth = 0.8
    ) +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
    labs(
        title = "Bivariate Normal Contours by Species (Palmer Penguins)",
        x = "Body Mass (g)",
        y = "Flipper Length (mm)",
        color = "Species"
    ) +
    theme_bw(base_size = 13) + 
    theme(legend.position="bottom")
```

Let's ignore Chinstrap penguins for a bit and focus on a binary Adelie *vs*
Gentoo classifier: 


```{r}
#| echo: false
# TODO: Fix this up. AI over complex nonsense follows...
library(tidyverse)
library(mvtnorm)

# 1. Clean data and define grid bounding box
df <- penguins |>
    drop_na(body_mass, flipper_len, species) |>
    filter(species != "Chinstrap")

grid_x <- seq(min(df$body_mass) - 200, max(df$body_mass) + 200, length.out = 150)
grid_y <- seq(min(df$flipper_len) - 5, max(df$flipper_len) + 5, length.out = 150)
eval_grid <- expand_grid(body_mass = grid_x, flipper_len = grid_y)

# 2. Fit 2D normal parameters (MLE) per species and evaluate density on the grid
density_df <- df |>
    nest(.by = species) |>
    mutate(
        mu = map(data, \(d) colMeans(d[, c("body_mass", "flipper_len")])),
        sigma = map(data, \(d) cov(d[, c("body_mass", "flipper_len")])),
        grid = map2(mu, sigma, \(m, s) {
            eval_grid |>
                mutate(density = dmvnorm(eval_grid, mean = m, sigma = s))
        })
    ) |>
    select(species, grid) |>
    unnest(grid)

# 3. Plot contours with observations
ggplot() +
    geom_point(
        data = df,
        aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len, color = species),
        alpha = 0.45,
        size = 1.5
    ) +
    geom_contour(
        data = density_df,
        aes(x = body_mass, y = flipper_len, z = density, color = species),
        bins = 7,
        linewidth = 0.8
    ) +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
    labs(
        title = "Bivariate Normal Contours by Species (Palmer Penguins)",
        x = "Body Mass (g)",
        y = "Flipper Length (mm)",
        color = "Species"
    ) +
    theme_bw(base_size = 13) + 
    theme(legend.position="bottom")
```

Clearly, points closer to the 'core' of the Adelie region (bottom-left, green)
are more likely to be Adelie and points closer to the top-right are more likely
to be the larger Gentoo penguins. Can we build this into a formal classification
rule? Indeed, we can!

Key idea: normal distribution probabilities are based on _distances_ (norms)
so being 'closer' to the core of one set increases our confidence for that class.
Different normal distributions just screw around with how we actually measure 
distance.

[^mle]: *Many* statistical procedures you have seen before are instances of
this sort of MLE with a suitable model. The sample mean is the MLE for estimating
the mean of a normal distribution, OLS is the MLE for a Gaussian linear model, 
*etc.*
